# On the Quiet Art of Paying Attention

There's a moment that happens almost every day, usually in the afternoon when the light slants through windows at that particular angle that makes everything look like it's made of amber and memory. I'll be doing something mundane—washing dishes, walking to the mailbox, sitting in traffic—and suddenly I'll notice something I've seen a hundred times before as if for the first time. The way water beads on a ceramic plate. The specific geometry of shadows under a mailbox door. The particular shade of frustration on someone's face in the car ahead of me.

These moments feel like small gifts, though I'm not entirely sure who's giving them to me, or whether I'm giving them to myself by finally pausing long enough to receive them.

I've been thinking a lot lately about attention, which is to say I've been thinking about presence, and presence is really just another word for love, though we don't usually admit that. We talk about attention as if it's a resource we manage, the same way we manage time or money. We speak of "paying" attention, which is interesting because it implies both a cost and a transaction. But I think attention is less like currency and more like oxygen—it's everywhere, we need it constantly, and we barely notice it until we're gasping for lack of it.

The pandemic did something to how I experience attention. I think it did this to a lot of people, though we don't always talk about it in these terms. We talk about it being "weird" or "surreal," but what we're really talking about is how it stripped away so many of the automatic, unconscious patterns of paying attention that we'd developed. Suddenly, there were fewer places to direct our focus. The world got smaller, squeezed into a few rooms, a few daily routines.

And in that smaller world, things became vivid.

I found myself noticing the way light moved across my kitchen table throughout the day. I could track time by it, almost. And I started to understand, in a way I never had before, that this is what monks were doing. That's what meditation is—a deliberate practice of directing attention inward, or toward the present moment, or toward whatever chosen object of focus. It's not mystical, though it can feel that way. It's just attentiveness made practice.

But here's what troubles me about our current moment, and what I've been wanting to write about: we're living in a time of radical attention fragmentation. Our devices don't just compete for our attention; they're designed specifically to hack it, to break it into smaller and smaller pieces. There's an entire industry built on the science of keeping our minds fractured, scattered, reaching for the next notification like a pigeon pecking at seeds on a floor.

This has a cost. I don't just mean the obvious costs—the mental health impacts, the loneliness despite constant connection, the anxiety, the sense of time slipping away. Though those are real. I mean something deeper. I mean the cost to our capacity for intimacy. Because intimacy, real intimacy, requires a kind of complete attention that has become genuinely rare.

When you give someone your complete attention—not just your eyes, but your mind, your nervous system, your presence—you're doing something radical. You're saying, through your actions rather than your words, that they matter more right now than anything else in the world. You're saying that this moment, this conversation, this person is worthy of your full self. In our current age, this has become nearly an act of resistance.

I think about this when I'm with friends, and I notice how hard it is to be fully present. Even when my phone is in another room, there's a kind of mental residue left behind. Fragments of attention still catching on the emails I didn't send, the messages I haven't read, the way the internet constantly hums in the background of consciousness. It's like trying to hear someone speak while music plays faintly in the distance—you can do it, but it takes effort that shouldn't be required.

There's a practice called "deep reading" that's supposed to be disappearing. I think what's actually disappearing is the capacity for sustained attention more generally. The research suggests that reading long-form prose, in particular, requires a kind of attention muscle that atrophies if you don't use it. But I think the same is true for listening, observing, being present in conversation. These are all skills, and like any skill, they require practice and can be lost through disuse.

What worries me is that we're raising a generation with underdeveloped attention muscles. I'm not being alarmist—the research is pretty clear on this. Rates of anxiety, depression, and ADHD diagnoses have risen dramatically, particularly among young people. Now, correlation isn't causation, and there are many factors at play. But I can't help but think that when your basic neurological wiring is trained from infancy to expect novelty every few seconds, to respond to interruptions as if they might be urgent, to understand that attention itself is a commodity to be sold to the highest bidder—that has to do something to you.

And yet. And yet, I'm not interested in writing some preachy jeremiad about phones and technology. That's been done, and honestly, it misses the point. The problem isn't the technology itself, any more than the problem with alcohol is the existence of wine. The problem is how we've chosen to use these tools, and the incentive structures that have been built around them.

What I'm interested in is the other side of this: what attention practices might look like for people living in this fractured age. Not "go sit in a monastery," but something more practical. Something that acknowledges that we live in the world as it is, not as we wish it were.

One thing I've started doing is taking what I call "attention walks." It's not exercise, though I'm walking. It's not meditation, though it shares some qualities with meditation. It's simply a deliberate walk through a familiar place—my neighborhood, usually—with the specific intention of really looking. Not looking at my phone, not thinking about where I need to be or what I need to do. Just noticing.

I notice the way a particular fence has weathered. The different colors of green in the plants along a single street. The small signs of people's lives—a child's drawing in a window, a garden gnome that's fallen over, the way someone has arranged rocks in a garden, presumably for beauty or to prevent erosion or both. These are not profound observations. But the act of making them feels profound. It feels like I'm practicing presence. Like I'm building the capacity to be here, really here, in my own life.

Another thing I've noticed: writing this way, by hand, feels different than typing. The pace is slower. There's less editing happening in real-time. Your thoughts come out more roughly, more truly. There's a kind of attention required in handwriting that typing has made optional. You have to commit to the word by putting it down. It creates a different relationship with your own thoughts.

I think this is why people are increasingly drawn to "analog" practices—journaling by hand, reading physical books, cooking from scratch. It's not really about the analog-ness, I don't think. It's about the pace. It's about the kind of attention that these practices require and cultivate.

Here's something I've been wanting to say for a while: I think the fundamental spiritual or philosophical question of our time is not "what is the meaning of life?" but rather "where do I place my attention?" Because where you place your attention is literally where your life happens. Your attention is your life, in a very real sense. Every moment that passes—and they are all passing—is a moment of your attention placed somewhere. Spent on something. Given to someone or something or somewhere.

This is why the current attention economy bothers me so much. It's not just that it's making us anxious or distracted. It's that it's training us to give our attention—which is to say, our lives—to people and things and causes that we don't actually care about. We're being literally harvested for our attention by companies whose business model depends on us not being present to our own lives.

And the weird part is, I don't think even the people designing these systems are necessarily trying to be evil. I think they're caught in the same system, the same incentive structures. But the system itself is structured in a way that's deeply at odds with human flourishing.

So what do you do with that knowledge? You can't opt out entirely. You can't go live in a cabin in the woods and pretend the world works differently now. Well, you could, but most of us won't, and maybe that's not even the right answer anyway.

I think what you do is you start small. You notice. You practice. You develop what might be called "attention hygiene"—small, deliberate choices about where you place your focus. You read a book without your phone in the room. You have a conversation without checking the time obsessively. You take a walk and actually look at things. You sit with a cup of tea and just sit with it, for a few minutes, without doing anything else.

These sound small because they are. But small practices become habits, and habits shape the underlying architecture of your mind and your life.

I've been thinking too about how attention relates to gratitude. You can't really feel gratitude for something you're not paying attention to. Gratitude isn't something you can fake or force—it emerges naturally when you actually notice the things you have. The meal in front of you. The person you're talking to. The fact that you got to see another sunset. That you have a body that can walk. That the sky is this particular shade of blue today.

This is why practices of attention and practices of gratitude are so closely linked in contemplative traditions. They're almost the same thing, viewed from different angles. When you attend to something with real focus, with real presence, gratitude naturally follows. You can't really be fully present to something without appreciating it, at least a little.

There's a writer I admire named Annie Dillard who wrote about this. She said something like: how we spend our days is how we spend our lives. The implication being that most of us are not very conscious about how we spend our days, so we're living unconsciously. And that if you want to live differently, to live more meaningfully or more fully, you need to start paying attention to how you actually spend your time. You need to wake up to your own life.

I think that's maybe the deepest thing that attention is about. It's about waking up. Being awake to your own existence while you're having it, rather than sleepwalking through it, reaching the end and wondering where the time went.

The pandemic taught me something about this. When everything stopped, when all the normal ways of staying busy and distracted were unavailable, I had to actually be present to the life I was living. And what I found was that it was enough. The small things were enough. The quiet morning, the afternoon light, the particular texture of a particular day. These were not nothing. They were everything.

I'm trying to hold onto that knowledge now that the world has largely restarted its normal pace. I'm trying to keep remembering that attention is not just a practical thing, not just about being more productive or less stressed (though it might be those things too). It's about being alive. It's about the quality of being alive. It's about the difference between existing and actually living.

And maybe that's what I want to say, in the end. That paying attention is not a productivity hack. It's not about doing more things or doing things better. It's about doing fewer things with more presence. It's about choosing, consciously and repeatedly, to be here now. To put your whole self into whatever you're doing, whoever you're with, whatever moment you're having.

Because this moment, this one, right now—it's the only one you're actually having. The rest are memories or fantasies. This one is real, and it's passing, and there's nothing else there.
